1.pericope_label: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles

schools.summary: Carry the suspended nominative past the whole digression and locate its resumption at the bowing of the knees rather than the plea against fainting; supply the missing verb so that Paul is the prisoner, following Tindale and a line of translators, and read the chains as proof of the mission rather than an interruption of it.

Turn the imprisonment into evidence. Christ's glory converts what the world counts a reproach into the highest honour, so that the chains of a prisoner of Jesus Christ outrank the crowns of kings; and since the suffering was for no capital crime and was borne on the Ephesians' own account, it confirms the doctrine rather than discrediting it.

Supply the history — the Jews persecuted Paul to bonds for admitting Gentiles without circumcision, whence Caesarea, the appeal, and Rome — and read the phrase "for you Gentiles" as meaning for their advantage and for the assertion of their right to these blessings.

Offer both readings of the opening phrase without choosing, and press the pastoral consequence: Christ's servants, when imprisoned, are his prisoners, and he thinks no worse of them for the character the world gives them.

debates.question: Where does the sentence broken off at the opening resume?

sides.position: At “I bow my knees”, on the strength of the repeated “for this cause” and the greater weight of that sentence
At the opening of the chapter, the intervening verses being a digression
Paul may have begun the prayer here and been diverted into the paragraph that follows

outliers.note: Alone suggests that Paul began the closing prayer here and was diverted by his own words into the long paragraph that follows.

2.pericope_label: If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward: how that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery, as I wrote afore in few words, whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ

schools.summary: Treat the conditional particle as assuming what it appears to question, and weigh the three candidates for what Paul "wrote afore" — this letter, a lost letter, or the two foregoing chapters — inclining to the last, and correcting "in few words" to mean briefly rather than shortly before.

Take the dispensation as the doctrine of grace rather than an inward gift, and defend the appeal to revelation against two abuses: the fanatics who ascribe their own dreams to the Spirit, and the sneer that a lost apostolic letter leaves Scripture mutilated — the surviving canon being no accident but a body adjusted by the counsel of God.

Render the particle "seeing that," since the Ephesians had learned all this while Paul was among them, and defend the reading "was made known" from a long list of manuscripts, versions and fathers, so that the doctrine is shown to rest on revelation and not on Paul's opinion.

debates.question: What does “as I wrote afore in few words” refer to?

sides.position: The two foregoing chapters
An earlier letter now lost

outliers.note: Alone argues from the lost letter to the integrity of the canon, holding that what survives is not an accident of transmission but a body adjusted by the counsel of God.

themes: the lost letter and the canon

5.pericope_label: Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit: that the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel, whereof I was made a minister

schools.summary: Read "the sons of men" as an Old Testament phrase deliberately set against the "holy" apostles, where holiness marks official call rather than character; identify the prophets as those of the Christian church and infer that their office lapsed once the written revelation was complete; and count the three fellow- compounds as late, rare, and in one case unique.

Answer the objection that the prophets had already foretold the calling of the nations by distinguishing the fact from its time and manner: the apostles themselves, who had both the predictions and their Master's word, still recoiled from the Gentile mission because the manner was hidden; and the older revelation lay in types, shadows and short obscure hints.

Insist on what was genuinely new — not that the Gentiles would be called, which the prophets had made clear, but that they should be saved without the yoke of the Mosaic law and the Jews freed from it; and press the Ezekiel echo in "son of man."
Cite the verse not as exposition but as proof, among a catena of texts, that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives, speaks and foretells.

debates.question: Had the calling of the Gentiles been made known before?

sides.position: The fact was foretold, but the time and manner were left undetermined, so that even the apostles recoiled from it
The calling was clear in the prophets; what was wholly new was salvation without the yoke of the Mosaic law
It was known only in types, shadows and short obscure hints

outliers.note: Alone infers from the verse that the prophetic office was temporary, ceasing when the written revelation was complete.
His block is not exposition of this verse but a catechetical lecture that cites it among proofs of the Spirit’s personality.

themes: what was hidden and what was new

8.pericope_label: Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ

schools.summary: Analyse the coined comparative built on a superlative — a form unparalleled in the New Testament though not unknown in later Greek — and trace "unsearchable" to the metaphor of tracking footsteps that cannot be followed to their source; but enter the caution that the self-abasement was not mock humility, since Paul defended his apostolic rights when occasion required.

Take the confession as sincere against the suspicion of feigned humility, while confining it to what Paul was in himself apart from grace; and generalise it — the greatest saints are the most humble, having the largest discoveries of grace and the keenest sense of their own vileness.

Explain the manufacture of the word and decline to better the received rendering; refer the untrackable footsteps to God's own plans and providences, and observe that Paul's letters in chronological order show his views brightening as he advances, so that he could never have exhausted the subject.

Make the phrase the lesson of the day, weighing it against "not meet to be called an apostle" and finding this the stronger self-abasement, the more remarkable for coming after so many great and good deeds.
Add the pastoral edge: many are not enriched with these riches, yet it is a great favour to have them preached and offered, and if we are not enriched the fault is our own.

debates.question: Is the self-abasement to be taken at face value?

sides.position: Yes, and it is the strongest of all Paul's self-descriptions, the more so for coming after his greatest labours
Yes as to what he was in himself, but it is not mock humility, since he defended his apostolic rights when occasion required

outliers.note: Alone weighs this self-description against the parallel in Corinthians and judges this the stronger of the two.

9.pericope_label: And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Prefer "dispensation" to "fellowship" on manuscript authority, referring it to the order God has ordained for manifesting the truth to men and angels; reject "by Jesus Christ" as a gloss imported from Colossians; and distinguish enlightening, which ministry can do, from making men see, which is the Spirit's work alone.

Hold that ministers enlighten instrumentally and God efficiently, and that "all men" means some of all sorts; hear in the metaphor a claim that grace now shines at noon-day, and rebuke the impatience that resents God's right to keep his purposes concealed until he pleases to reveal them.

Marshal the versions and fathers for the better reading and pronounce the closing clause indisputably spurious, drawing the doctrinal moral at once — no inferiority of Christ can be argued from a clause so poorly attested.

debates.question: Is the true reading “fellowship” or “dispensation” of the mystery?

sides.position: “Dispensation”, on manuscript, versional and patristic authority
“Fellowship” retains a real sense — the doctrine now common to all believers, against the reserved doctrines of the pagan mysteries

debates.question: Are the words “by Jesus Christ” genuine?

sides.position: Spurious, a gloss imported from the parallel in Colossians
Read as genuine, and referred to the spiritual renewal rather than the first creation

outliers.note: Alone contrasts the passage with the pagan mystery religions, following Whately, to argue that Christianity has no reserved doctrines and no truths entrusted to a priesthood alone.

10.pericope_label: To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God, according to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord

schools.summary: Take the principalities as angels who learn from the church, so that this world may be a lesson to spheres of being beyond our conception; render "manifold" as many-coloured and find the variety in the church's teaching and life; and reject the reading of "eternal purpose" as an arrangement of ages, insisting that God has a plan and that any plan of his must be eternal.

Deny that the words can be shifted to devils, since nothing remarkable would be said in informing them; make the church a mirror in which angels see a wisdom new to them, while refusing the inference that angels attend our assemblies; and rebuke the narrowness that measures God's wisdom by one dispensation only.

Canvass three identifications of the principalities and report Macknight's, that the angelic orders learn as the dispensations unfold; read "manifold" as multifarious, plans laid on an infinite scale and accomplished by endless means that no malice can defeat; and take the eternal purpose as a purpose concerning the periods.

debates.question: Who are the principalities and powers?

sides.position: The good angels, who learn the manifold wisdom of God from the church
Possibly evil angels, or the converted Jewish rulers and rabbins
A purpose concerning the periods — the appointed span of the Jewish and gospel dispensations
A purpose eternal in the proper sense; the alternative is at variance with the settled use of the word and evades the doctrine that God has a plan

outliers.note: Alone rejects the inference that angels attend Christian assemblies and grow in knowledge alongside the congregation.
Names Clarke among the expositors he is refuting — one of the few places in this corpus where one witness rebuts another by name.

12.pericope_label: In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him. Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory

schools.summary: Distinguish the two gifts — boldness of utterance before men and angels, and confident access before God as sons rather than servants — each resting on a different aspect of faith; settle the genitive as objective; and correct the account of what the Ephesians were in danger of, which was discouragement at a faith that exposed its friends to such calamities, not doubt of its truth.

Define faith by its fruits in three stages — belief of the promise, the trust that rests on it, and the confidence that banishes fear — holding that to separate confidence from faith is to take heat and light from the sun, so that a doubting conscience is evidence of unbelief; and admire the pastor who draws comfort from prison for those in no danger.

Picture the access as a petitioner brought before the king by a favourite and the boldness as a child's freedom with an indulgent father; insist that we come only in Christ's name, which is why prayers are closed in it; and reduce the last clause to five words — the not fainting is your glory.
Notice that Paul seems more anxious lest the believers be discouraged by his tribulations than about what he had himself to bear.

debates.question: What danger were the Ephesians in from Paul's imprisonment?

sides.position: Losing heart in a religion that exposed its friends to such calamities
Concluding that the religion itself was vain and false

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a definition of faith in three stages and applies it against the schoolmen who enjoin hesitation in prayer.

14.pericope_label: For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ

schools.summary: Prefer a reference to the verse immediately preceding over a resumption of the opening, summarise the prayer as moving from the Spirit's strengthening to the indwelling of Christ and on to the fulness of God, judge "of our Lord Jesus Christ" an interpolation from a gloss, and doubt that Paul knelt as he dictated.

Explain why the prayer is reported — to stir the readers to pray likewise, since the seed of the word is scattered in vain unless God makes it fruitful — and draw the lesson for ministers: the Spirit's work does not make instruction superfluous but gives it weight, and is no excuse for sloth.
Take the verse as resuming what was begun in the opening, and read the gesture as an outward expression owed to the reverence the heart should feel in drawing near to God.

Turn the posture into a rebuke of those who sit or stand at prayer, arguing from the respect paid to a man of rank or a king, and find in the whole prayer a second dedication, Paul kneeling as Solomon did to dedicate the Christian church.

sides.position: It is the proper posture, and its abandonment in the churches is to be regretted
The gesture is indifferent; the heart is the thing, though reverence commonly expresses itself so

outliers.note: Alone turns the posture into a sustained rebuke of contemporary congregations, and alone reads the prayer as a dedication of the Christian church answering Solomon’s at the temple.
His block is a catechetical lecture on the blinding of unbelievers and has no bearing on this verse.

15.pericope_label: Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named, that he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man

schools.summary: Report the division over the antecedent, weigh and reject the rendering "fatherhood" on grounds of usage, and read "family" as any body of rational beings united under a common fatherhood and bearing its ancestor's name; then distinguish this petition from the earlier one as asking strength rather than light, and for the whole inner man rather than the eyes of the heart.

Refer "of whom" to Christ rather than the Father, since referring it to the Father revives the very distinction the passage abolishes; make union to the body of Christ the one relationship that counts in heaven and earth; and deny that any believer advances so far as to need no further growth.

Take the Father as the antecedent without argument; press the singular "family" against the notion that each order forms its own household; and call the petition one of the most sublime in the whole of Scripture, measured by God's own infinite fulness as a king gives according to his dignity.
Quote the verse in passing among proofs that the Spirit of the Father, the Comforter and the Spirit of truth are one under different titles.

sides.position: To Christ, since referring it to the Father revives the very Jew–Gentile distinction the passage abolishes
To the Father
Either is possible

debates.question: Should the noun be rendered “family” or “fatherhood”?

sides.position: “Every family” — the rendering “fatherhood” is tempting but contrary to usage
The singular is deliberate: one family, not many households

outliers.note: His column here carries an editorial note credited to Chandler, setting the “whole family” against the federation of Asiatic cities united in the worship of Diana of Ephesus — material that is not Calvin’s own.

17.pericope_label: That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love

schools.summary: Identify the indwelling of Christ with the gift of the Spirit rather than making it a consequence, faith being simply the condition; gloss the verb as making oneself at home; place the two participles with the following clause; and deny that love is the root or foundation, which is Christ, love being the condition of growth.

Distinguish this personal indwelling from omnipresence and from a merely spiritual presence, and bind Spirit and Christ inseparably together; insist that fellowship with Christ follows faith rather than being identical with it, since faith is not a distant view but a warm embrace; and refuse the inference that love is the foundation of salvation.

Read the whole through the figure of the temple — man made God's dwelling, defiled and abandoned, repaired by Christ — with the warning that a heart which is not God's house will be a hold of unclean spirits; and take the double metaphor as agriculture and architecture together.

debates.question: Is love the root and foundation spoken of?

sides.position: No — the foundation is Christ himself; love is the condition under which growth takes place
The metaphors are simply of firmness, love being the soil and the ground alike

outliers.note: Alone breaks off to observe that a deal of fixing would be needed in our hearts before Christ could be at home in them.

18.pericope_label: May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height; and to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God

schools.summary: Hold that Paul deliberately left the four dimensions without a noun, so that no supplement is fully satisfactory; refuse the easy resolution of the paradox by opposing spiritual to head-knowledge, reading the tense instead as knowing from time to time what in its entirety always exceeds discovery; and correct "filled with" to "filled up to" the fulness of God.

Dismiss Augustine's cruciform allegory and Ambrose's sphere and take the dimensions to mean simply the love of Christ, which contains the whole of wisdom; contend against the schoolmen that the certainty of faith is real knowledge though taught by the Spirit; and warn against reading the fulness as an equality with God.

Reject the allusion to the temple of Diana in favour of the temple at Jerusalem, and refuse to soften the closing clause by inserting the word "communicable" — Paul means what he says, and what God fills neither sin nor Satan can fill.

debates.question: Of what are the breadth, length, depth and height?

sides.position: Of nothing specified — Paul left the phrase deliberately incomplete
Of the love of Christ
Of the spiritual temple, by allusion to the temple at Jerusalem rather than that of Diana
Possibly of the temple of Diana at Ephesus, or of the calling of the Gentiles
Of the cross, its four dimensions figuring love, hope, patience and humility

debates.question: How can what passes knowledge be known?

sides.position: The tense means knowing from time to time what in its entirety always exceeds discovery; there is no opposition of spiritual to head-knowledge
The verb may mean to acknowledge or approve; or the knowledge surpassed is rabbinic and Greek science
It is simply the language of a heart full to overflowing

outliers.note: Alone names and dismisses the patristic readings of the four dimensions, calling Augustine’s cruciform allegory ingenious and entertaining but beside Paul’s meaning.

20.pericope_label: Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen

schools.summary: Note the rare double compound and the middle voice of the asking; render the closing formula literally as all the generations of the age of the ages, each generation adding its thanksgiving to a chorus filling eternity; and turn the chapter's doctrine against every attempt to confine the gospel to a favoured caste, ancestry, complexion or class.

Define the power as exerted rather than viewed apart from its act, and set out its limits — God cannot do what contradicts his nature or his decrees; locate the rendering of glory in the church, where alone the mysteries of grace are known; and give the striking permission that faith of the proper kind need fear no excess.

Climb the gradation of asking, thinking, and beyond both, and bind God's ability to his willingness, since power without willingness would be no comfort to the church; and close with an estimate of the chapter as unequalled in the New Testament for matter and sublimity.
State the rule the passage teaches — that it is proper always to end prayer with praise, and to expect and ask for more on the strength of what Christ has already done.

debates.question: How far may the closing clause be pressed?

sides.position: At full strength — inserting “communicable” to soften it is idle and impertinent
Not to an equality with God, which would be a foolish and wicked dream
The preposition is “up to” rather than “with”, so the clause describes conformation to Christ's image

outliers.note: Alone qualifies the doxology by naming what God cannot do — whatever contradicts his nature or his decrees.
Appends remarks turning the chapter against exclusion by caste, ancestry, wealth and complexion, naming the doctrine that a lighter skin marks the favourite of heaven and dooms others to servitude.
